newsitem.title: CROATIA: Tudjman speech awaited, could herald changes.
newsitem.headline: Tudjman speech awaited, could herald changes.

text.p: Croatia's ailing President Franjo Tudjman delivers a keenly-awaited speech on Wednesday amid speculation that the authoritarian 74-year-old might announce constitutional changes or even herald his own retirement.

Croatians are eagerly awaiting the annual "State of the Nation" address, to be delivered to parliament probably in the morning and televised nationally, believing it might throw light on the way ahead for the former Yugoslav republic.
Reports published in independent Croatian media in recent weeks said the nationalist leader, who according to U.S. sources has incurable cancer, could announce constitutional changes.
The weekly Globus said Tudjman would cancel a presidential vote due in the second half of 1997 and call for constitutional changes to pave the way for a parliamentary system.

The weekly Nacional said he might even announce his retirement and introduce a constitutional amendment transferring the mandate for presidential powers to parliament, which would directly elect the head of state.

But a senior presidential aide quoted by Globus played down such anticipation, saying the speech would be "much softer than many expect" and adding: "It will not contain crucial political decisions that the public has been speculating about."

"There has been a lot of speculation but I don't think he (Tudjman) will announce (big) changes. The changes they are considering are rather cosmetic, linguistic changes, not affecting the constitutional set-up," he told Reuters.
Nevertheless, the speech may help to illuminate the way ahead for Croatia under unusual circumstances -- the illness of a long unchallenged leader coupled with his party's declining popularity.

Since its 1991 secession from federal Yugoslavia, Croatia has had a semi-presidential system dominated by the charismatic, strongman figure of Tudjman, who has exercised his authority in all areas of life.

But since his treatment for reported cancer at a U.S. hospital in November, rumours have swirled that Tudjman is terminally ill and some diplomats have said he would only have a months before having to retire from duty.

Some analysts believe his Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ) party, its popularity waning over alleged corruption and mismanagement of the economy, may be manoeuvring to put off presidential elections should Tudjman feel too ill to run.

In that case the HDZ, which holds a majority in parliament, would effectively rule Croatia at least until 1999, when parliamentary elections are due, even if its grip slackened through expected losses in March regional elections.
Tudjman, looking gaunt from weight loss, unusually dropped from sight for more than a week early this month but re-emerged looking better and moving more easily.
The presidential cabinet issued a statement saying he was making a good recovery and "with the people's and God's will he will continue to perform his duties for some time to come".

After a six-month war with minority Serbs opposing its independence in 1991, Croatia in 1995 recaptured two rebel enclaves and the third, Easstern Slavonia, is due to return peacefully to Zagreb rule this year.
